sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

passages.text: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .

The SVD is computed only every τ \tau steps to amortize the computational cost. After each refresh, the principal states m ∥ m^{\parallel} and v ∥ v^{\parallel} are rewritten in the new basis with the transport rule of LDAdam ( Robert et al., 2024 ) (Appendix A ). Only these r × r r\times r states need transport, because M t M_{t} and its residual are defined in the original parameter space. By storing the momentum M t M_{t} in BF16 and confining adaptive states to the compact coordinate representation, the dominant persistent-state cost of ResQAdam is 2 ​ n ​ m 2nm bytes, with an additional O ⁡ ( ( n + m ) ​ r + r 2 ) O((n+m)r+r^{2}) overhead for the bases and principal states. For r ≪ min ⁡ ( n , m ) r\ll\min(n,m) this approaches 25% of AdamW. The measured reduction is 71% to 74% (Section 4 ), mainly because the bases are not negligible for the smaller matrices. Figure 2: Training loss trajectories of ResQAdam and AdamW during from-scratch QAT under various quantization configurations on the 430M-parameter LLM. The values following the optimizer names in the legend indicate the average memory footprint of the optimizer states.

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Values in each cell are formatted as AdamW / ResQAdam , with relative changes in parentheses. AdamW / ResQAdam Llama 3.2-1B Qwen2.5-1.5B Qwen3 4B-Base Opt. State Memory (GB) 7.78 / 2.16 ( ↓ \downarrow 72.2%) 10.48 / 3.01( ↓ \downarrow 71.3%) 29.07 / 7.78 ( ↓ \downarrow 73.2%) Total Peak Memory (GB) 33.33 / 28.24 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 43.93 / 37.19 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 99.14 / 79.77 ( ↓ \downarrow 19.5%) Throughput (# token/s) 29.36k / 28.94k ( ↓ \downarrow 1.4%) 18.31k / 18.19k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.6%) 9.64k / 9.56k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.8%) To evaluate hardware efficiency, we compare ResQAdam against AdamW in terms of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput. These results show that our amortized update strategy substantially alleviates the optimizer-state memory bottleneck of QAT while maintaining competitive training throughput.

Table 4: Perplexity comparison of memory-efficient optimizers under diverse QAT paradigms and quantization configurations. Projection-based optimizers use rank 64. Training Paradigm Q-Cfg ResQAdam GaLore-AdamW GaLore-AdamW8bit LDAdam AdaFactor From-Scratch QAT W2A16G128 20.05 30.61 30.39 28.57 33.01 W4A4G128 18.89 32.93 32.45 28.23 32.84 QAT Fine-Tuning W2A16G128 16.89 19.25 20.32 19.59 27.79 W4A4G128 15.05 15.30 15.64 15.42 14.80 We further compare ResQAdam with two families of memory-efficient optimizers. Structural factorization methods such as AdaFactor ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) keep the full parameter dimensionality but approximate the second moment by row and column statistics. Table 4 reports the average perplexity on WikiText-2 and C4. This is consistent with our hypothesis that confining the update to a low-rank subspace, or replacing the second moment by a factorized approximation, loses part of the correction that QAT relies on. In fine-tuning the picture depends on the bit width. At W2A16G128 the projection-based methods remain clearly behind, whereas at W4A4G128, where quantization error is small, all optimizers land within a narrow range and the choice of optimizer matters little.

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly used in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), often under similar optimizer settings. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. passages.text: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton–Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton–Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton–Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four. † † shortheadings: Finite-Depth Newton–Schulz Dynamics / Long † † firstpage: 1 † † heading: 2026 1–

Another question concerns the extent to which small-initialization asymptotics can determine the subsequent training trajectory. Under suitable structural conditions, gradient flow admits a precise description in which the initialization scale can be used to reverse-engineer the full training dynamics, leading also to a characterization of time-dependent implicit regularization ( Berthier, 2023 ) . For finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics, the nonlinear matrix iteration prevents this reconstruction argument from carrying over directly. Although the dynamics can be analyzed in a small neighborhood of the origin, the resulting local description does not by itself determine the trajectory after leaving that neighborhood. This creates two distinct dynamical scales: the entrance dynamics near the origin and the subsequent evolution away from it. Establishing how the entrance dynamics are transmitted to the later trajectory is one of the main results of this paper.

Following the framework of Li et al. (2021) , which characterizes the first nonzero stationary point selected by gradient flow under suitable assumptions, we study the evolution from small initialization through the first stationary point encountered after escape. This allows us to compare the stationary points approached by gradient descent and by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics. Under an additional structural assumption, we establish a sufficient large-depth guarantee: for all sufficiently large spectral depths, the selected Newton–Schulz continuation approaches a first stationary point whose loss is strictly smaller than that of the first stationary point selected by gradient descent. For smaller depths, our results do not provide a general criterion determining whether the trajectory visits or bypasses the gradient-descent stationary point. Moreover, without the additional assumption, the first stationary points reached by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics and gradient descent may have the same loss. Such equal-loss behavior may reveal further dynamical structures, which we leave for future work. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model and pathwise comparison criteria. Sections 3–5 establish the Gaussian entrance law, continuation criteria, and eventual depth guarantee. Section 6 presents an exact empirical task, and Section 7 discusses the scope of the results and open questions. Detailed proofs are given in the appendices.

In this paper, we have studied how finitely many iterations of a nonlinear matrix transformation can reshape optimization dynamics. In a quadratic two-layer network, we have characterized the evolution from small-initialization escape near the origin to the first nonzero stationary stage. Our results provide a precise description of how the number of Newton–Schulz iterations controls early rank selection and regulates the subsequent optimization path. passages.text: Distributed learning has become a core paradigm for modern machine learning systems, spanning data-parallel training, federated learning, and edge learning scenarios where computation and data are spread across multiple nodes. In such settings, optimization algorithms must handle stochastic gradient noise, statistical heterogeneity, and communication constraints. While a large body of prior work studies these issues for conventional vector-based methods such as SGD [ 9 ] and Adam [ 21 ] , these methods treat parameters as flat vectors. Much less is understood when parameters and gradients are naturally matrix-valued, as in Transformers and convolutional networks. Recently, Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization (SSBO) methods, such as Muon [ 16 ] , Shampoo [ 13 ] , and SOAP [ 49 ] , have attracted growing attention for their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network updates. Among them, Muon has garnered the most interest due to its exceptional efficiency in large language model (LLM) training. Muon also has a relatively simple implementation: it orthogonalizes a matrix-valued momentum before applying the update, yielding geometry-aware descent directions [ 28 , 15 ] . Despite the promise of these SSBO methods, both their theory and implementation remain largely confined to centralized training in the literature, leaving open the question of how they should be designed and analyzed in distributed settings.

However, developing SSBO-based methods for distributed learning is highly non-trivial due to several technical challenges. First , the nonlinear spectral mapping does not commute with distributed aggregation. Averaging locally transformed spectral directions is generally not equivalent to applying the spectral map after aggregating the underlying momentum estimates, which can introduce systematic bias. Second , data heterogeneity and noisy gradient estimates further exacerbate this nonlinearity challenge. In distributed stochastic training, deviations in the momentum estimators are coupled with the nonlinear spectral mapping and can lead to directional errors, suggesting that the matrix-valued estimator should be carefully controlled before applying the spectral map. Third , practical Muon-style implementations typically replace exact orthogonalization with finite-step Newton–Schulz (NS) iterations. The resulting approximation error must therefore be explicitly accounted for in the convergence analysis. Fourth , synchronizing full matrix-valued momentum variables incurs substantial communication cost. This high communication cost motivates low-rank communication, whose additional approximation error must also be carefully controlled. In this work, we focus on Muon-type SSBO algorithmic framework and propose the Distributed Momentum-based Spectral Estimator ( 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} ) method, a unified framework for distributed SSBO. The key idea of 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} is to build a variance-reduced distributed SSBO backbone as the foundation for practical Newton-Schulz orthogonalization and communication-efficient low-rank synchronization. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• A variance-reduced Distributed SSBO Backbone: We first develop 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} with exact orthogonalization and full communication of matrix-valued momentum. A STORM-style recursive estimator controls the stochastic deviation of the matrix-valued momentum before the nonlinear spectral transformation. Under the stated assumptions, 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} achieves an O ( ( K T ) − 1 / 3 ) O((KT)^{-1/3}) convergence rate for averaged stationarity, where K K and T T denote the number of nodes and local optimization iterations per node, respectively, matching the best-known rates for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization. • 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} with Finite-step Newton-Schulz Orthogonalization: We replace the exact orthogonalization step with a finite number of Newton-Schulz (NS) iterations and show that the same O ( ( K T ) − 1 / 3 ) O((KT)^{-1/3}) convergence order is preserved under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, up to a multiplicative approximation factor. • Communication-efficient Low-rank Implementation: We extend 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} to a low-rank communication-efficient implementation, where nodes can transmit low-rank momentum factors instead of full matrices. We quantify the additional error introduced by low-rank communication through an additive accumulated term accounting for both client and server spectral truncation.

1) Dataset and Setting. We evaluate 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} on CIFAR-10 [ 24 ] using a widened ResNet-20 with Group Normalization. Distributed learning has become a core paradigm for modern machine learning systems, spanning data-parallel training, federated learning, and edge learning scenarios where computation and data are spread across multiple nodes. In such settings, optimization algorithms must handle stochastic gradient noise, statistical heterogeneity, and communication constraints. While a large body of prior work studies these issues for conventional vector-based methods such as SGD [ 9 ] and Adam [ 21 ] , these methods treat parameters as flat vectors. Much less is understood when parameters and gradients are naturally matrix-valued, as in Transformers and convolutional networks. Recently, Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization (SSBO) methods, such as Muon [ 16 ] , Shampoo [ 13 ] , and SOAP [ 49 ] , have attracted growing attention for their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network updates. Among them, Muon has garnered the most interest due to its exceptional efficiency in large language model (LLM) training. Muon also has a relatively simple implementation: it orthogonalizes a matrix-valued momentum before applying the update, yielding geometry-aware descent directions [ 28 , 15 ] . However, developing SSBO-based methods for distributed learning is highly non-trivial due to several technical challenges. First , the nonlinear spectral mapping does not commute with distributed aggregation. Averaging locally transformed spectral directions is generally not equivalent to applying the spectral map after aggregating the underlying momentum estimates, which can introduce systematic bias. Second , data heterogeneity and noisy gradient estimates further exacerbate this nonlinearity challenge. In distributed stochastic training, deviations in the momentum estimators are coupled with the nonlinear spectral mapping and can lead to directional errors, suggesting that the matrix-valued estimator should be carefully controlled before applying the spectral map. Third , practical Muon-style implementations typically replace exact orthogonalization with finite-step Newton–Schulz (NS) iterations. The resulting approximation error must therefore be explicitly accounted for in the convergence analysis. Fourth , synchronizing full matrix-valued momentum variables incurs substantial communication cost. This high communication cost motivates low-rank communication, whose additional approximation error must also be carefully controlled. passages.text: MapHub, the MIDAS arXiv Preprint Hub, assesses each day’s new arXiv submissions for every participant in a research community, with a large language model reading each paper against portfolios built for the participants. It publishes the relevance scores, from 0 to 100, as a heatmap that shows whose work each paper touches. In the authors’ blind ratings, the top 10% of papers by MapHub’s scores held about 70% of the raters’ own top 5%, pooled, against about a third for a text-matching baseline. About 6% of a day’s astro-ph papers reach 30 for each participant, and one every three days reaches 60. MapHub runs on a standard Claude subscription and is designed to be useful for any field: https://github.com/kailicao/maphub-public .

Nowadays, each arXiv announcement brings about ninety new astro-ph submissions, and readers cannot attend to all of them equally [ 4 ] . myADS runs keyword and author queries on new preprints [ 5 ] ; recommenders learn a reader’s interests from topics, text similarity, or ratings [ 6 , 3 ] , or adapt inspectable profiles day by day [ 8 ] . Open-source projects use large language models to rank each day’s listing against one reader’s interests, and at Ohio State, agents built from 21 faculty members’ publication records each discuss matching daily papers [ 7 ] . These tools serve one reader at a time, or share discussions, rather than publishing how each paper relates to each member. MapHub 1 1 1 https://kailicao.github.io/maphub-public/ combines three things: Every new paper is scored for every participant and shown in one heatmap, one row per paper and one column per participant; the profiles are portfolios that participants can check and correct themselves; the scores are public and traceable.

A public prompt can be used to draft each participant’s research portfolio from a publication record, and the participant checks it: about 1,500–3,000 words, built from their own papers and plans, listing methods and targets as well as topics. Portfolios stay among participants and the model’s provider; scores are public, as participants agree when they join. Claude Opus 5.5 [ 1 , at low effort;] reads each new paper’s title, authors, and abstract against the portfolios and returns a relevance score from 100 (“the participant wrote the paper, or would”) through 60 (“would cite it”) and 30 (“it may broaden their view”) to 0, a fit to the portfolio rather than a judgment of quality. MapHub assesses new submissions to its listings (here astro-ph and cs.AI; the listings can be configured). Since most cells score low, a first pass scores chunks of about 50 papers for all participants at once against short outlines of the portfolios, and only papers scoring 10 or more are rescored against a full portfolio. On two test listings (748 papers), this cost about 36% of a single full pass and missed none of the 56 cells that pass scored 40 or more. The prompts, code, and tables are public, scores are labeled as AI-generated, and each table’s commit records what produced it, so the output can be checked. Figure 1: (a) An example day of MapHub, as its viewer shows it: the 23 papers (of 262) that reached 30 for some participant on 2026 August 25, numbered by average score. (b), (c) The share of each rater’s top 5% (b) and top 15% (c) found, against the share of astro-ph papers read in order of score. Columns are pooled and weighted back to uniform sampling; bands are 68% bootstrap intervals.

Seventy listings scored with version 0.8’s portfolios and prompt held 11,932 new submissions, scored for one individual, two groups, and two collaborations. Of a day’s 87 astro-ph papers, 6.3 % ± 3.5 % 6.3\%\pm 3.5\% (mean ± \pm standard deviation) reach 30 for each participant and 0.4% reach 60. Even the individual column, spanning multiple subfields, sees only 7 ± 3 7\pm 3 astro-ph papers a day at 30 or more: minutes of reading abstracts. And 8% of astro-ph papers reach 30 for two or more participants (Figure 1 a). Of a day’s 84 cs.AI papers, about two reach 30 for the individual, and almost none for the others. To test whether the scores save time, the authors rated one shared list blind for themselves or their groups on MapHub’s rubric, each interpreting its descriptions in their own way. 2 2 2 One rater recast its descriptions as a scale from 1 to 5. Only each rater’s order is used. The list held 45 astro-ph papers drawn with probabilities rising with a paper’s highest score ( ∝ 2 s / 20 \propto 2^{s/20} ), five of them shown twice, and 10 cs.AI papers spanning the individual column’s scores. Papers by the participants were left out; the portfolios were fixed on 2026 October 14 and cite none of the rated papers. Each rating is weighted by the inverse of its paper’s chance of being drawn, so the results estimate what reading these listings would find. A paper counts as of interest if it is in the rater’s top 5% (or 15%) of the population by their own ratings.

Reading in MapHub’s order finds the rater’s top 5% quickly (Figure 1 b): MapHub’s top 5% of papers hold about a third of it, and its top 10% about 70%, against 33% for a term-frequency baseline (TF-IDF 3 3 3 https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer.html of title and abstract against the portfolio) reading the same share. MapHub’s lead is 39 points at 10% read (95% interval: 11–60; ahead in every bootstrap draw). The top 15% is spread more widely: MapHub’s top 10% holds about a third of it, against about 20% for TF-IDF, and the two converge when about 40% of the listing is read (Figure 1 c). MapHub’s cutoff of 30 means reading 4%–9%, and over 90% of the papers above it were in the rater’s top 15%.

A department’s heatmap could help an Astro Coffee-style discussion 4 4 4 https://astronomy.osu.edu/coffee of the whole listing: Papers touching several columns are natural topics, and their highest-scoring participants natural people to ask. Portfolios drawn from publication records may miss interests not yet published: The groups’ portfolios name machine learning only as a tool for their science, so MapHub may miss AI papers their members want. Adding these interests to the portfolios would fix this; meanwhile, the individual’s column flags AI papers. Scores stay comparable across days, since every paper is read against the portfolio on one rubric, and rescoring changed them by 1.7 points on average. MapHub is still under development, and the test is small. Its ratings are subjective: The first author, who built the tool, rated three of the five columns, and a rating shifts with the papers read just before it. Each rater’s top 5% holds few papers, and defining interest by percentile assumes every rater has some. It publishes the relevance scores, from 0 to 100, as a heatmap that shows whose work each paper touches. In the authors’ blind ratings, the top 10% of papers by MapHub’s scores held about 70% of the raters’ own top 5%, pooled, against about a third for a text-matching baseline. About 6% of a day’s astro-ph papers reach 30 for each participant, and one every three days reaches 60. MapHub runs on a standard Claude subscription and is designed to be useful for any field: https://github.com/kailicao/maphub-public .

Nowadays, each arXiv announcement brings about ninety new astro-ph submissions, and readers cannot attend to all of them equally [ 4 ] . myADS runs keyword and author queries on new preprints [ 5 ] ; recommenders learn a reader’s interests from topics, text similarity, or ratings [ 6 , 3 ] , or adapt inspectable profiles day by day [ 8 ] . Open-source projects use large language models to rank each day’s listing against one reader’s interests, and at Ohio State, agents built from 21 faculty members’ publication records each discuss matching daily papers [ 7 ] . These tools serve one reader at a time, or share discussions, rather than publishing how each paper relates to each member. MapHub 1 1 1 https://kailicao.github.io/maphub-public/ combines three things: Every new paper is scored for every participant and shown in one heatmap, one row per paper and one column per participant; the profiles are portfolios that participants can check and correct themselves; the scores are public and traceable.

A public prompt can be used to draft each participant’s research portfolio from a publication record, and the participant checks it: about 1,500–3,000 words, built from their own papers and plans, listing methods and targets as well as topics. Portfolios stay among participants and the model’s provider; scores are public, as participants agree when they join. Claude Opus 5.5 [ 1 , at low effort;] reads each new paper’s title, authors, and abstract against the portfolios and returns a relevance score from 100 (“the participant wrote the paper, or would”) through 60 (“would cite it”) and 30 (“it may broaden their view”) to 0, a fit to the portfolio rather than a judgment of quality. MapHub assesses new submissions to its listings (here astro-ph and cs.AI; the listings can be configured). Since most cells score low, a first pass scores chunks of about 50 papers for all participants at once against short outlines of the portfolios, and only papers scoring 10 or more are rescored against a full portfolio. On two test listings (748 papers), this cost about 36% of a single full pass and missed none of the 56 cells that pass scored 40 or more. The prompts, code, and tables are public, scores are labeled as AI-generated, and each table’s commit records what produced it, so the output can be checked. Figure 1: (a) An example day of MapHub, as its viewer shows it: the 23 papers (of 262) that reached 30 for some participant on 2026 August 25, numbered by average score. (b), (c) The share of each rater’s top 5% (b) and top 15% (c) found, against the share of astro-ph papers read in order of score. Columns are pooled and weighted back to uniform sampling; bands are 68% bootstrap intervals.

Seventy listings scored with version 0.8’s portfolios and prompt held 11,932 new submissions, scored for one individual, two groups, and two collaborations. Of a day’s 87 astro-ph papers, 6.3 % ± 3.5 % 6.3\%\pm 3.5\% (mean ± \pm standard deviation) reach 30 for each participant and 0.4% reach 60. Even the individual column, spanning multiple subfields, sees only 7 ± 3 7\pm 3 astro-ph papers a day at 30 or more: minutes of reading abstracts. And 8% of astro-ph papers reach 30 for two or more participants (Figure 1 a). Of a day’s 84 cs.AI papers, about two reach 30 for the individual, and almost none for the others. To test whether the scores save time, the authors rated one shared list blind for themselves or their groups on MapHub’s rubric, each interpreting its descriptions in their own way. 2 2 2 One rater recast its descriptions as a scale from 1 to 5. Only each rater’s order is used. The list held 45 astro-ph papers drawn with probabilities rising with a paper’s highest score ( ∝ 2 s / 20 \propto 2^{s/20} ), five of them shown twice, and 10 cs.AI papers spanning the individual column’s scores. Papers by the participants were left out; the portfolios were fixed on 2026 October 14 and cite none of the rated papers. Each rating is weighted by the inverse of its paper’s chance of being drawn, so the results estimate what reading these listings would find. A paper counts as of interest if it is in the rater’s top 5% (or 15%) of the population by their own ratings.

Reading in MapHub’s order finds the rater’s top 5% quickly (Figure 1 b): MapHub’s top 5% of papers hold about a third of it, and its top 10% about 70%, against 33% for a term-frequency baseline (TF-IDF 3 3 3 https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer.html of title and abstract against the portfolio) reading the same share. MapHub’s lead is 39 points at 10% read (95% interval: 11–60; ahead in every bootstrap draw). The top 15% is spread more widely: MapHub’s top 10% holds about a third of it, against about 20% for TF-IDF, and the two converge when about 40% of the listing is read (Figure 1 c). MapHub’s cutoff of 30 means reading 4%–9%, and over 90% of the papers above it were in the rater’s top 15%.

A department’s heatmap could help an Astro Coffee-style discussion 4 4 4 https://astronomy.osu.edu/coffee of the whole listing: Papers touching several columns are natural topics, and their highest-scoring participants natural people to ask. Portfolios drawn from publication records may miss interests not yet published: The groups’ portfolios name machine learning only as a tool for their science, so MapHub may miss AI papers their members want. Adding these interests to the portfolios would fix this; meanwhile, the individual’s column flags AI papers. Scores stay comparable across days, since every paper is read against the portfolio on one rubric, and rescoring changed them by 1.7 points on average. MapHub is still under development, and the test is small. Its ratings are subjective: The first author, who built the tool, rated three of the five columns, and a rating shifts with the papers read just before it. Each rater’s top 5% holds few papers, and defining interest by percentile assumes every rater has some. passages.text: Scaled weight decay for Muon (Muon-SW) has been reported to train language models more efficiently than constant decoupled weight decay, but such comparisons usually reuse one learning-rate (LR) and weight-decay (WD) setting for both methods. We re-run the comparison under the MAI-Base-2 protocol: LR and WD are tuned jointly through their product for each method, on a source-scaled mixture-of-experts (MoE) scaling ladder (1.9M to 15M active parameters) that holds tokens per active parameter and data repetition fixed across sizes. We find: (1) Most of the gain is a tuning gap. At the shared setting Muon-SW wins by 0.035 0.035 bits per byte (BPB), a 1.52 × 1.52\times compute saving. After both methods are tuned, the gap is 0.0026 0.0026 BPB (95% CI [ 0.0018 , 0.0034 ] [0.0018,0.0034] ), a 1.03 × 1.03\times saving: about 90% of the advantage disappears. (2) The small advantage that remains is real. At the smallest size, all four paired seeds favour Muon-SW at the tuned settings. (3) That advantage grows with model size. Across an 8 × 8\times range of active parameters, the tuned gap rises from 0.0036 0.0036 to 0.0051 0.0051 BPB while the untuned gap shrinks from 0.035 0.035 to 0.024 0.024 , so the share of the advantage that survives tuning rises from about 10% to 21%. (4) The best weight decay moves with scale. The optimal LR ⋅ \cdot WD product grows for both methods, faster for Muon-SW (ratio 1.40 → 1.91 1.40\to 1.91 ). A law fitted on the two smallest sizes overshoots the third by 1.3 1.3 – 1.5 × 1.5\times , costing up to 0.002 0.002 BPB. The whole study runs on one NVIDIA T4 GPU; we release the code and all run results.

New optimizer variants are commonly evaluated by training a model with the variant and with a baseline, at one shared set of hyperparameters, and reporting the difference. When the variant changes how strongly a hyperparameter acts—as a weight-decay schedule does—the shared setting can be well tuned for one method and poorly tuned for the other, and part of the reported gain is then a tuning gap. This concern is old ( Choi et al., 2019 , Dahl et al., 2023 ) , but it is sharper for weight decay, whose effect is coupled to the learning rate ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 , Kosson et al., 2023 , Wang and Aitchison, 2024 ) and whose optimum moves with model and data size. Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) is now used for the hidden-layer matrices of large language models ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , including the 2.8T parameter MAI-Base-2 ( Microsoft AI, 2026 ) . Apte (2026) propose scaling Muon’s weight-decay coefficient over training (Muon-SW) and report gains over constant decay. MAI-Base-2 introduced two practices that make a cleaner test possible. First, LR and WD are swept jointly on a grid in (LR, LR ⋅ \cdot WD), because good settings lie on a narrow diagonal of the (LR, WD) plane and a 2D quadratic fit gives the optimum. Second, models are compared on a scaling ladder with fixed tokens per active parameter (TPP) and source scaling , which keeps the number of repetitions of every data source fixed across rungs so that small models do not favour under-regularised settings. We ask one question: how much of Muon-SW’s advantage survives once the baseline is tuned as carefully as the method, and how does that share change with scale? Our contributions are:

• A tuned comparison of Muon-SW and constant decay under the MAI-Base-2 LR ⋅ \cdot WD protocol on a source-scaled MoE ladder (three rungs, 1.9M to 15M active parameters, 81 completed runs). • The finding that about 90% of Muon-SW’s untuned advantage disappears after joint tuning at the smallest rung (survival 7.4 % 7.4\% in the full 2D analysis, 10.3 % 10.3\% in the 1D slice), but that the residual is consistent across seeds and grows with scale (survival 10 % → 13 % → 21 % 10\%\to 13\%\to 21\% ). • Measurements of how the optimal LR ⋅ \cdot WD product moves with scale for each method, a test of three preregistered predictions for the ratio of optima, and an out-of-sample check of the fitted law at L6. • A pre-emption-safe pipeline that runs the full ladder on one T4 GPU.

For each rung, the untuned gap is the constant-decay BPB minus the Muon-SW BPB, both at p = 1 p=1 ; the tuned gap is the difference between the two methods’ tuned BPB. Survival is tuned gap divided by untuned gap. At L3 we also convert gaps into a compute-equivalent speedup with the loss-versus-compute fit used by our analysis pipeline.

Table 1: Main result. Untuned gap : constant-WD BPB minus Muon-SW BPB, both at the MAI-law setting ( p = 1 p=1 ). Tuned gap : the same difference after each method is tuned over the LR ⋅ \cdot WD multiplier p p (quadratic fit in log 2 ⁡ p \log_{2}p ). Survival = tuned gap / untuned gap. p ⋆ p^{\star} is the fitted optimal multiplier; Ratio is p SW ⋆ / p const ⋆ p^{\star}_{\rm SW}/p^{\star}_{\rm const} . Upper block: one-dimensional sweep at learning-rate multiplier 1 for every rung. Lower block: the full two-dimensional (LR × \times LR ⋅ \cdot WD) L3 analysis, confirmed by four paired seeds at the fitted optima. † Fitted optimum lies outside the sampled range; the tuned BPB is the better of the fitted and best observed value. All BPB values are on held-out data. Table 2: Measured ratio of optimal LR ⋅ \cdot WD products (Muon-SW over constant decay) at L3, with bootstrap 95% intervals, against the three preregistered predictions (§ 3.4 ). Under the cosine schedule the data are consistent with no change and with matched integrated decay, and rule out endpoint matching. Under WSD the ratio falls below every prediction. Figure 1: Held-out BPB against the LR ⋅ \cdot WD multiplier p p (log scale) for each rung. Points are runs; curves are quadratic fits in log 2 ⁡ p \log_{2}p ; dotted lines mark fitted optima; the dashed line marks the MAI-law setting p = 1 p=1 . At p = 1 p=1 Muon-SW (orange) is far better, but constant decay (blue) recovers most of the gap by moving to a smaller p p .

Most of the advantage reported for Muon’s scaled weight decay is a tuning gap: when constant decay’s LR ⋅ \cdot WD product is tuned as carefully as the method’s, about 90% of the gain disappears at small scale. What remains is small but consistent, and it grows with model size, from about 10% to 21% of the untuned gap across an 8 × 8\times range of active parameters, while the optimal products of the two methods move apart. Optimizer comparisons should tune the baseline at every scale they report, and claims about scaled weight decay should be made from tuned comparisons at the target scale.

2611.08414:a79f85041669e5b4e522c9df9c23c.question: Which language models, mathematical-reasoning tasks, learning rates, and controlled SFT-versus-RL comparisons support the reported spectrum and subspace differences? What baselines and measured task-quality results support the proposed SFT spectrum flattening and RL updates?

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly used in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), often under similar optimizer settings. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks across multiple models show that the respective configurations for SFT and RL yield the best performance among the compared methods in most evaluated settings.

passages.section: The dynamics inform stage-specific LoRA optimization (Section 4 ).
passages.text: Our analysis further shows which dynamics accompany the risk-favorable learning rate: training without a baseline (as in SFT) expands the spectrum of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} , whereas training with a baseline (as in RL) concentrates the spectrum and rotates the left singular subspace faster. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor the update of LoRA factors to each stage by combining two standard components, a norm-preserving spectral flattening as in Muon [ 14 ] and a per-factor choice between SGD and Adam update directions. In SFT, we flatten the singular spectrum of the full update of the factor so that the adaptation is distributed more evenly across singular directions; whereas in RL, we flatten only the component of the update orthogonal to the current left singular subspace of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} , which promotes subspace rotation while leaving the within-subspace component unchanged. The resulting configurations achieve dominating downstream performance across most evaluated models and tasks.

passages.section: Differences between supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning.
passages.text: Prior work has characterized differences between SFT and RL at the output, representation, and parameter levels. At the output level, empirical studies report stronger out-of-distribution performance under RL than SFT [ 18 , 5 ] . Subsequent work further highlights the dependence of SFT generalization on optimization, data quality, and model capability [ 29 ] . Beyond performance, studies examine the diversity of generated outputs: RLHF reduces overall response diversity relative to SFT [ 18 ] , while analyses distinguishing correct and incorrect reasoning trajectories find that SFT expands the former and RL compresses the latter [ 21 ] . Moreover, a line of work examines how changes in the model’s output distribution during fine-tuning relate to the preservation of pretrained capabilities. These studies illustrate how on-policy RL can better preserve distributional modes associated with prior knowledge than SFT [ 4 ] , and link RL’s better retention to an implicit preference for output distributions closer to that of the initial model in KL divergence [ 34 ] . At the hidden representation level, Shi et al. [35] find that SFT rapidly introduces specialized features that stabilize early, whereas RL induces more restrained but continually evolving feature changes.

passages.section: Differences between supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning.
passages.text: At the parameter update level, studies report greater sparsity in parameter updates under RL than SFT [ 24 ] . Comparisons of update vectors across tasks reveal large absolute cosine similarities under SFT, whereas RL updates are nearly orthogonal [ 50 ] . Spectral analyses of the weight matrices further show smaller changes from the pretrained spectra and principal subspaces under RLVR than SFT [ 49 ] . Our work also compares spectral and subspace dynamics under SFT and RL. In contrast, we focus on the LoRA update matrix itself, track how its spectral concentration and subspace rotation vary with learning rate and training step, interpolate between SFT and RL through intermediate training settings to identify where these differences arise, and use these findings to guide the choice of optimizer configurations for LoRA in each paradigm.

As shown in Tables 1 and 2 , while applying ℳ \mathcal{M} to the full B B update with Adam directions does not consistently improve over standard Adam, the dynamics-informed configuration for SFT further replaces the Adam direction for B B with SGD and achieves the highest reported mean accuracy across all evaluated models and tasks. These comparisons highlight the benefit of combining spectral flattening with asymmetric optimization of the two LoRA factors.

In this work, we identify distinct spectral and subspace dynamics of LoRA under SFT and RL. Our experiments show that RL effective rank consistently decreases during training across the learning rates considered, while for models that benefit from SFT, the growth of effective rank accompanies better SFT performance at intermediate learning rates. In addition to this difference in spectral dynamics, RL exhibits faster subspace rotation than SFT at small learning rates, with the gap narrowing as the learning rate increases. Controlled comparisons identify group-mean baseline subtraction as a key source of these differences. Using a multi-index model, our theoretical framework analyzes how baseline subtraction changes coherent fitting and feedback from gradient noise, jointly shaping effective rank, subspace rotation, and learning-rate preferences in prediction risk. These insights guide the choice of two dynamics-informed configurations for LoRA optimization, tailored to the distinct training dynamics of SFT and RL. Both configurations achieve the highest reported mean accuracy in most evaluated settings.

passages.text: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA is governed by rank, which controls parameter budget and locally accessible task updates. Existing dynamic-rank methods mainly focus on capacity allocation, leaving unresolved whether the current adaptation space is sufficient for the task. We characterize the first-order information boundary of standard factor gradients, showing that their unobservable subspace coincides with the normal space of the low-rank manifold. Thus, factor gradients alone cannot distinguish under-optimization within the current space from task-relevant directions beyond its first-order reach. This motivates a geometric view of rank evolution, where tangent information optimizes existing degrees of freedom and the normal spectrum quantifies the value of new ones. Under a local quadratic model, we show that leading normal singular directions yield the locally optimal rank expansion, with spectral energy determining its gain. Building on this characterization, we propose GEAR, which turns the tangent–normal decomposition into rank evolution through tangent-space optimization, matrix-free normal-spectrum estimation for rank expansion, and task-induced geometric initialization. Across language and vision benchmarks, GEAR achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters. On LLaMA3-8B, it raises the average commonsense score from 86.61 to 88.45 while reducing trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.

We introduce GEAR, which unifies optimization over the current fixed-rank manifold and rank expansion using tangent information to optimize the adaptation space and the normal spectrum to identify and value new task-relevant directions. • Excellent performance–parameter trade-off. We established a first-order information boundary for standard factor gradients, showing that task-relevant normal information is unobservable from the current fixed-rank parameterization, and further related the normal spectrum to the locally optimal value of rank expansion. Building on this analysis, GEAR combines fixed-rank manifold optimization, efficient normal-spectrum estimation, and task-induced geometric initialization to adapt rank according to task-relevant directions beyond the current first-order reachable space. Across commonsense reasoning, GLUE, and VTAB-1K, GEAR achieves the highest average performance in all evaluated settings while using substantially fewer trainable parameters than strong adaptive-rank baselines. Overall, our results suggest that dynamic rank is most effectively viewed not as a budget-allocation problem alone, but as the controlled evolution of the adaptation space in response to previously unrepresented task information.

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

Fine-tuning changes the behavior of a pretrained model by writing an update relative to what that model already knows. How many bits are actually required to preserve this acquired behavior? Parameter count, adapter rank, and numerical precision measure storage, but need not measure the information that matters functionally. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) provides a clean setting for studying this question: the base model remains frozen while the learned update is isolated in a separate adapter that can be compressed after training. We take a receiver-relative rate–distortion view of this process. As illustrated in Figure 1 , fine-tuning acts as an encoder, the adapter as a finite-rate message, and the frozen model as side information available when that message is decoded. We measure rate by the exact serialized size of a compressed adapter and distortion by the behavior of the resulting composed model. For a fixed retention target, the behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} is the smallest measured rate that preserves the required fraction of the held-out fine-tuning gain. This operational definition exposes a gap between numerical and behavioral compression. Lower weight reconstruction error need not preserve more learned behavior, and comparable bit budgets can have different effects depending on where compression acts. Behavioral rate also increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budget. Most importantly, the same datasets can require substantially different rates across frozen models, with their ordering changing across receivers. A correction-gradient spectrum computed from the data and receiver ranks R ⋆ R^{\star} well within a fixed receiver, but does not transfer reliably across new receivers. Singular-direction analyses show that harmful and useful effects are distributed unevenly across the update, while matched-norm controls show that the recovery is not exactly equivalent to scalar rescaling. passages.text: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton–Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton–Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton–Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four. † † shortheadings: Finite-Depth Newton–Schulz Dynamics / Long † † firstpage: 1 † † heading: 2026 1–

Another question concerns the extent to which small-initialization asymptotics can determine the subsequent training trajectory. Under suitable structural conditions, gradient flow admits a precise description in which the initialization scale can be used to reverse-engineer the full training dynamics, leading also to a characterization of time-dependent implicit regularization ( Berthier, 2023 ) . For finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics, the nonlinear matrix iteration prevents this reconstruction argument from carrying over directly. Although the dynamics can be analyzed in a small neighborhood of the origin, the resulting local description does not by itself determine the trajectory after leaving that neighborhood. This creates two distinct dynamical scales: the entrance dynamics near the origin and the subsequent evolution away from it. Establishing how the entrance dynamics are transmitted to the later trajectory is one of the main results of this paper.

Following the framework of Li et al. (2021) , which characterizes the first nonzero stationary point selected by gradient flow under suitable assumptions, we study the evolution from small initialization through the first stationary point encountered after escape. This allows us to compare the stationary points approached by gradient descent and by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics. Under an additional structural assumption, we establish a sufficient large-depth guarantee: for all sufficiently large spectral depths, the selected Newton–Schulz continuation approaches a first stationary point whose loss is strictly smaller than that of the first stationary point selected by gradient descent. For smaller depths, our results do not provide a general criterion determining whether the trajectory visits or bypasses the gradient-descent stationary point. Moreover, without the additional assumption, the first stationary points reached by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics and gradient descent may have the same loss. Such equal-loss behavior may reveal further dynamical structures, which we leave for future work. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model and pathwise comparison criteria. Sections 3–5 establish the Gaussian entrance law, continuation criteria, and eventual depth guarantee. Section 6 presents an exact empirical task, and Section 7 discusses the scope of the results and open questions. Detailed proofs are given in the appendices.

passages.text: Distributed learning has become a core paradigm for modern machine learning systems, spanning data-parallel training, federated learning, and edge learning scenarios where computation and data are spread across multiple nodes. In such settings, optimization algorithms must handle stochastic gradient noise, statistical heterogeneity, and communication constraints. While a large body of prior work studies these issues for conventional vector-based methods such as SGD [ 9 ] and Adam [ 21 ] , these methods treat parameters as flat vectors. Much less is understood when parameters and gradients are naturally matrix-valued, as in Transformers and convolutional networks. Recently, Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization (SSBO) methods, such as Muon [ 16 ] , Shampoo [ 13 ] , and SOAP [ 49 ] , have attracted growing attention for their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network updates. Among them, Muon has garnered the most interest due to its exceptional efficiency in large language model (LLM) training. Muon also has a relatively simple implementation: it orthogonalizes a matrix-valued momentum before applying the update, yielding geometry-aware descent directions [ 28 , 15 ] . Despite the promise of these SSBO methods, both their theory and implementation remain largely confined to centralized training in the literature, leaving open the question of how they should be designed and analyzed in distributed settings.

However, developing SSBO-based methods for distributed learning is highly non-trivial due to several technical challenges. First , the nonlinear spectral mapping does not commute with distributed aggregation. Averaging locally transformed spectral directions is generally not equivalent to applying the spectral map after aggregating the underlying momentum estimates, which can introduce systematic bias. Second , data heterogeneity and noisy gradient estimates further exacerbate this nonlinearity challenge. In distributed stochastic training, deviations in the momentum estimators are coupled with the nonlinear spectral mapping and can lead to directional errors, suggesting that the matrix-valued estimator should be carefully controlled before applying the spectral map. Third , practical Muon-style implementations typically replace exact orthogonalization with finite-step Newton–Schulz (NS) iterations. The resulting approximation error must therefore be explicitly accounted for in the convergence analysis. Fourth , synchronizing full matrix-valued momentum variables incurs substantial communication cost. This high communication cost motivates low-rank communication, whose additional approximation error must also be carefully controlled. In this work, we focus on Muon-type SSBO algorithmic framework and propose the Distributed Momentum-based Spectral Estimator ( 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} ) method, a unified framework for distributed SSBO. The key idea of 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} is to build a variance-reduced distributed SSBO backbone as the foundation for practical Newton-Schulz orthogonalization and communication-efficient low-rank synchronization. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• A variance-reduced Distributed SSBO Backbone: We first develop 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} with exact orthogonalization and full communication of matrix-valued momentum. A STORM-style recursive estimator controls the stochastic deviation of the matrix-valued momentum before the nonlinear spectral transformation. Under the stated assumptions, 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} achieves an O ( ( K T ) − 1 / 3 ) O((KT)^{-1/3}) convergence rate for averaged stationarity, where K K and T T denote the number of nodes and local optimization iterations per node, respectively, matching the best-known rates for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization. • 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} with Finite-step Newton-Schulz Orthogonalization: We replace the exact orthogonalization step with a finite number of Newton-Schulz (NS) iterations and show that the same O ( ( K T ) − 1 / 3 ) O((KT)^{-1/3}) convergence order is preserved under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, up to a multiplicative approximation factor. • Communication-efficient Low-rank Implementation: We extend 𝖣𝗂𝗌𝖬𝖴𝖲𝖤 \mathsf{DisMUSE} to a low-rank communication-efficient implementation, where nodes can transmit low-rank momentum factors instead of full matrices. We quantify the additional error introduced by low-rank communication through an additive accumulated term accounting for both client and server spectral truncation.

It publishes the relevance scores, from 0 to 100, as a heatmap that shows whose work each paper touches. In the authors’ blind ratings, the top 10% of papers by MapHub’s scores held about 70% of the raters’ own top 5%, pooled, against about a third for a text-matching baseline. About 6% of a day’s astro-ph papers reach 30 for each participant, and one every three days reaches 60. MapHub runs on a standard Claude subscription and is designed to be useful for any field: https://github.com/kailicao/maphub-public .

Nowadays, each arXiv announcement brings about ninety new astro-ph submissions, and readers cannot attend to all of them equally [ 4 ] . myADS runs keyword and author queries on new preprints [ 5 ] ; recommenders learn a reader’s interests from topics, text similarity, or ratings [ 6 , 3 ] , or adapt inspectable profiles day by day [ 8 ] . Open-source projects use large language models to rank each day’s listing against one reader’s interests, and at Ohio State, agents built from 21 faculty members’ publication records each discuss matching daily papers [ 7 ] . These tools serve one reader at a time, or share discussions, rather than publishing how each paper relates to each member. MapHub 1 1 1 https://kailicao.github.io/maphub-public/ combines three things: Every new paper is scored for every participant and shown in one heatmap, one row per paper and one column per participant; the profiles are portfolios that participants can check and correct themselves; the scores are public and traceable.

A public prompt can be used to draft each participant’s research portfolio from a publication record, and the participant checks it: about 1,500–3,000 words, built from their own papers and plans, listing methods and targets as well as topics. Portfolios stay among participants and the model’s provider; scores are public, as participants agree when they join. Claude Opus 5.5 [ 1 , at low effort;] reads each new paper’s title, authors, and abstract against the portfolios and returns a relevance score from 100 (“the participant wrote the paper, or would”) through 60 (“would cite it”) and 30 (“it may broaden their view”) to 0, a fit to the portfolio rather than a judgment of quality. MapHub assesses new submissions to its listings (here astro-ph and cs.AI; the listings can be configured). Since most cells score low, a first pass scores chunks of about 50 papers for all participants at once against short outlines of the portfolios, and only papers scoring 10 or more are rescored against a full portfolio. On two test listings (748 papers), this cost about 36% of a single full pass and missed none of the 56 cells that pass scored 40 or more. The prompts, code, and tables are public, scores are labeled as AI-generated, and each table’s commit records what produced it, so the output can be checked. Figure 1: (a) An example day of MapHub, as its viewer shows it: the 23 papers (of 262) that reached 30 for some participant on 2026 August 25, numbered by average score. (b), (c) The share of each rater’s top 5% (b) and top 15% (c) found, against the share of astro-ph papers read in order of score. Columns are pooled and weighted back to uniform sampling; bands are 68% bootstrap intervals.

Seventy listings scored with version 0.8’s portfolios and prompt held 11,932 new submissions, scored for one individual, two groups, and two collaborations. Of a day’s 87 astro-ph papers, 6.3 % ± 3.5 % 6.3\%\pm 3.5\% (mean ± \pm standard deviation) reach 30 for each participant and 0.4% reach 60. Even the individual column, spanning multiple subfields, sees only 7 ± 3 7\pm 3 astro-ph papers a day at 30 or more: minutes of reading abstracts. And 8% of astro-ph papers reach 30 for two or more participants (Figure 1 a). Of a day’s 84 cs.AI papers, about two reach 30 for the individual, and almost none for the others. To test whether the scores save time, the authors rated one shared list blind for themselves or their groups on MapHub’s rubric, each interpreting its descriptions in their own way. 2 2 2 One rater recast its descriptions as a scale from 1 to 5. Only each rater’s order is used. The list held 45 astro-ph papers drawn with probabilities rising with a paper’s highest score ( ∝ 2 s / 20 \propto 2^{s/20} ), five of them shown twice, and 10 cs.AI papers spanning the individual column’s scores. Papers by the participants were left out; the portfolios were fixed on 2026 October 14 and cite none of the rated papers. Each rating is weighted by the inverse of its paper’s chance of being drawn, so the results estimate what reading these listings would find. A paper counts as of interest if it is in the rater’s top 5% (or 15%) of the population by their own ratings.

Reading in MapHub’s order finds the rater’s top 5% quickly (Figure 1 b): MapHub’s top 5% of papers hold about a third of it, and its top 10% about 70%, against 33% for a term-frequency baseline (TF-IDF 3 3 3 https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer.html of title and abstract against the portfolio) reading the same share. MapHub’s lead is 39 points at 10% read (95% interval: 11–60; ahead in every bootstrap draw). The top 15% is spread more widely: MapHub’s top 10% holds about a third of it, against about 20% for TF-IDF, and the two converge when about 40% of the listing is read (Figure 1 c). MapHub’s cutoff of 30 means reading 4%–9%, and over 90% of the papers above it were in the rater’s top 15%.

A department’s heatmap could help an Astro Coffee-style discussion 4 4 4 https://astronomy.osu.edu/coffee of the whole listing: Papers touching several columns are natural topics, and their highest-scoring participants natural people to ask. Portfolios drawn from publication records may miss interests not yet published: The groups’ portfolios name machine learning only as a tool for their science, so MapHub may miss AI papers their members want. Adding these interests to the portfolios would fix this; meanwhile, the individual’s column flags AI papers. Scores stay comparable across days, since every paper is read against the portfolio on one rubric, and rescoring changed them by 1.7 points on average. MapHub is still under development, and the test is small. Its ratings are subjective: The first author, who built the tool, rated three of the five columns, and a rating shifts with the papers read just before it. Each rater’s top 5% holds few papers, and defining interest by percentile assumes every rater has some.
